hints: Look closely at the units in each option and convert them all to the same unit, remember that $1000 \text{ nm} = 1 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.
Recall the golden rule for 9700: prokaryotes (bacteria) are much smaller than eukaryotes, typically only a few micrometres across.
walkthrough:
**Remember the size of a prokaryote**

Think of a typical bacterium like E. coli. It is tiny, much smaller than an animal or plant cell.

A prepared student remembers this rule:
$$\text{prokaryotic cell} \approx 1 \text{ to } 5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$$

**Convert all options to micrometres**

This question mixes nm and um to test you, so convert using $1 \text{ } \mu\text{m} = 1000 \text{ nm}$.

Option A is $1 \text{ nm}$ to $500 \text{ nm}$, which is $0.001 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $0.5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. Option B is $1000 \text{ nm}$ to $5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, which is $1 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.

**Pick the match**

Only option B gives $1 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, the classic prokaryote range. Options C and D are in tens to thousands of micrometres, far too big for any cell of this type.

options.A: Too small. $1 \text{ nm}$ to $500 \text{ nm}$ is virus size or the size of small organelles, not a whole bacterial cell.
options.B: Correct. $1 \times 10^3 \text{ nm} = 1 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, so this is $1 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$, the typical prokaryotic range.
options.C: Too large. $10 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $500 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ fits many eukaryotic cells, not prokaryotes.
options.D: Far too large. $100 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ to $5000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ is visible to the naked eye and much bigger than any bacterium.
